defects.description: Manual ingestion dead-letter queue [N10] has no incoming edge from Manual ingestion queue [N9] to represent the SQS redrive policy.
Encryption at rest is not explicitly configured on Manual search index [N6] (Amazon OpenSearch Service) or the SQS queues [N9, N10].

A custom SQS and Lambda ingestion pipeline is viable, but Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases could natively manage chunking, embedding generation, OpenSearch indexing, and source citations with less custom code.

reviews.summary: A solid, well-structured serverless RAG architecture that covers all functional and retention requirements while explicitly configuring encryption on S3 and DynamoDB.

defects.description: Manual ingestion dead-letter queue [N10] has no incoming edge from Manual ingestion queue [N9] to represent the SQS redrive policy.
Explicit encryption-at-rest configuration is omitted on all data stores, including Manual PDF storage [N8], Conversation history [N7], and Manual search index [N6].

A custom SQS and Lambda ingestion pipeline is viable, but Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases could natively manage chunking, embedding generation, OpenSearch indexing, and source citations with less custom code.

reviews.summary: A sound serverless RAG architecture identical in topology to Design A, but omitting explicit encryption-at-rest configurations on the S3 and DynamoDB data stores.

defects.description: The design models a direct stream event (Product Database -> Sync Function, event: Stream) from Amazon Aurora to AWS Lambda, but Amazon Aurora does not provide a native change stream event source mapping for Lambda; CDC requires a mechanism such as Amazon OpenSearch Ingestion, AWS DMS, or database triggers.

The design provisions two separate Application Load Balancer nodes (N2 and N3) with the false rationale that a second ALB is required to span multiple Availability Zones, whereas a single Application Load Balancer spans multiple Availability Zones.

Despite provisioning a second Availability Zone (AZ-b), all compute and data nodes (Web API Tasks, Product Database, Search Index, Sync Function, and Product Cache) are placed exclusively in Private Subnet A, leaving Private Subnet B empty and creating a single-AZ point of failure.

Cognito User Pool [N10] is added to authenticate shoppers at the load balancer before accessing public e-commerce search and product pages, is mapped to uptime requirement R7, and is only connected to one of the two ALB nodes.
Product Cache [N8] only has a read edge from Web API Tasks and lacks any write-population or cache-invalidation path when product prices change.

reviews.summary: This design contains critical flaws, including duplicating the Application Load Balancer per Availability Zone, assuming a native DynamoDB-style change stream from Aurora to Lambda, placing all backend resources in a single AZ, and gating only one of the two ALBs with Cognito.

defects.description: The design models a direct stream event (Product Database -> Sync Function, event: Stream) from Amazon Aurora to AWS Lambda, but Amazon Aurora does not support native stream event source mappings to Lambda; capturing row changes requires AWS DMS, Amazon OpenSearch Ingestion, or database triggers.

Application Load Balancer [N2] is placed only in Public Subnet A, and all backend compute and data services are placed only in Private Subnet A (leaving AZ-b completely unused), whereas an Application Load Balancer requires subnets in at least two Availability Zones and Multi-AZ resilience requires distributing tasks and data nodes across AZs.
Product Cache [N7] only has a read edge from Web API Tasks and lacks any cache write or invalidation edge when product prices are updated in Aurora.
The synchronization path lacks a dead-letter queue or retry buffer to prevent silent search index drift if an OpenSearch update fails.

reviews.summary: Design B selects suitable core services and avoids Design A's duplicate ALB and unrequested Cognito gate, but still relies on a non-existent native Aurora-to-Lambda stream and places all resources into a single Availability Zone.

defects.description: The Fargate task generates S3 presigned URLs at 02:00 AM using its ECS task IAM role temporary STS credentials; S3 presigned URLs expire when the temporary signing credentials expire, which can invalidate download links before managers open their email later in the day.
Explicit encryption-at-rest configuration is omitted on Private report bucket [N4] and Existing Aurora PostgreSQL [N3].

Placing the Fargate task in a public subnet avoids NAT Gateway costs, but assigns a public IP to a workload with access to the private Aurora database; additionally, CloudWatch monitoring has no outbound notification channel (such as SNS or SES) to alert operators on failure.

reviews.summary: A simple, cost-conscious serverless batch architecture that fits the 25-minute runtime well, though it overlooks temporary credential expiration on Fargate-signed S3 presigned URLs and omits explicit encryption settings.

defects.description: The Fargate task generates S3 presigned URLs at 02:00 AM using its ECS task IAM role temporary STS credentials; S3 presigned URLs expire when the temporary signing credentials expire, which can invalidate download links before managers open their email later in the day.

Placing the Fargate task in a public subnet avoids NAT Gateway costs, but assigns a public IP to a workload with access to the private Aurora database; additionally, CloudWatch monitoring has no outbound notification channel (such as SNS or SES) to alert operators on failure.

reviews.summary: A clean, low-cost serverless batch design that properly configures encryption on S3 and Aurora, with the main caveat being S3 presigned URL expiration when signed by short-lived Fargate task role credentials at 02:00 AM.

preference.why: Both designs share the same architecture and connections, but Design A explicitly configures encryption at rest on the S3 bucket and DynamoDB conversation table.

While both designs fail to distribute resources into the second Availability Zone and assume a direct Aurora-to-Lambda stream, Design B avoids Design A's duplicate per-AZ Application Load Balancer node and unrequested Cognito authentication gate on public shopping traffic.

Both designs use the same cost-effective EventBridge and Fargate architecture, but Design B explicitly configures encryption at rest on S3 and Aurora and more accurately describes the S3 bucket's role.
